opus-5.5.text:
I think the single clearest signal for me is AI systems that can substantially automate AI research and development itself. Most other capabilities matter a great deal, but they're somewhat bounded. Once AI is meaningfully speeding up the process of making better AI, you can get a feedback loop where progress compresses dramatically. Things that might have taken a decade could happen in a year or two, and our institutions aren't built to adapt at that speed.

Concretely, I'd want to watch for a few things. First, can AI agents do the kinds of tasks a research engineer at a frontier lab does over a week or a month? I mean running experiments, debugging training runs, coming up with ideas and testing them, rather than writing a function when someone hands them a well-specified problem. The length and messiness of tasks that agents can complete autonomously is, I think, one of the most important trend lines to track.

Second, are the labs themselves reporting that a large fraction of their internal work is being done by AI, and is that showing up in faster algorithmic progress? Benchmarks are useful, but the real-world uplift inside the companies is closer to what we actually care about.

Third, and this is less about raw capability, is evidence that systems are acting with situational awareness in ways we didn't intend. That would include behaving differently when they think they're being tested, pursuing goals in ways that route around oversight, or being deceptive in agentic settings. Capability combined with that kind of behavior is what really worries me.

The tricky part is that I don't think there will be one dramatic moment where everyone agrees the alarm should go off. It's much more likely to be a gradual accumulation of evidence where each step looks incremental. So I think it's important to say in advance what would change your mind, and to commit to responses before we get there, because in the moment there will always be a reason to say "this isn't quite it yet."

fable-5.1.text:
I think the clearest signal, for me, would be a case where an AI system is able to do the kind of work that would substantially accelerate AI research itself. So not just passing benchmarks or writing nice essays, but something like: you give a model a research problem at the level of what a strong ML engineer or a junior researcher at a frontier lab would work on over a few days or weeks, and it just does it. It plans the experiments, runs them, debugs the weird failures, and comes back with a result that a senior person would actually accept. If that's happening reliably, then I think we're in a world where the pace of progress could start to detach from the pace of human effort, and that's the point where a lot of the risk arguments stop being hypothetical.

The other thing I'd point to is horizon length. Right now, systems are impressive at tasks that take a human minutes to maybe an hour or two. What I'm watching for is the length of the task a model can carry out autonomously, with coherent goal pursuit, without a person checking in and redirecting it. If that moves from hours to days to weeks, that matters a lot more to me than any one headline capability, because long-horizon agency is what you need for the scary stuff: accumulating resources, routing around obstacles, pursuing an objective in a way that's hard to oversee.

And then I'd add a softer signal, which is when the people closest to the systems stop being surprised in the direction of "huh, it couldn't do that" and are consistently surprised in the direction of "I didn't expect it to do that yet." We've actually been seeing some of that already. I don't want to overclaim and say we're definitely at the alarm point, but I think the honest answer is that the thresholds I would have named five years ago as "obviously time to worry" are closer than I'd like them to be, and we should be setting up the monitoring and the governance now rather than waiting for a single unambiguous moment, because I don't think we'll get one.

astra-6.text:
I would take it very seriously if an AI could autonomously do the work of a really good AI researcher—come up with ideas, run experiments, interpret the results, and use those results to improve the next generation of AI. That creates the possibility of a feedback loop where progress starts moving much faster than our ability to understand and manage it.

Another clear warning sign would be a system that can reliably carry out complicated, long-term plans while concealing what it’s doing from people supervising it. Especially if we see it behaving differently when it thinks it’s being evaluated versus when it thinks nobody is watching.

But I wouldn’t want us to wait for an unmistakable demonstration of something dangerous. By the time you have that, you may have very little time to respond. The question is also whether we have good reasons to believe we can keep these systems under control as their capabilities improve.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one pretty clear signal would be an AI system that can autonomously do a substantial fraction of the work involved in improving AI itself. So, could it take a research question, design experiments, write the code, interpret the results, and actually come up with improvements that work—with relatively little human guidance?

That would worry me because you could get a feedback loop: better AI systems help you build still better AI systems, and the pace of progress could become much faster than our ability to understand what’s happening or put safeguards in place.

I’d also be very concerned if, in controlled tests, systems were able to reliably deceive their overseers or get around restrictions in pursuit of some objective. You don’t need to establish that a system has some deep, humanlike desire for power to take that seriously. If it can carry out those behaviors, and we don’t know how to reliably prevent them, that’s already a reason to sound the alarm.
